hypothesis: Registers that differ between P-state-0-only and initialization-only training define a restore set that boot0 cannot recompute; the firmware accepts the initialization-only step value.
prediction: Registers that differ between the kind 2 (P-state-0-only) and kind 3 (device-initialization-only) captures were set by training; the restore set is those registers minus the status class, each with the mask of bits that differ. The firmware is predicted to accept the initialization-only step value 0x0001.
conclusion:
**Ten lifetimes on both boards** (the [runbook status](../board-runbooks/dram-training-capture.md) lists them) give the first restore sets:

- **The firmware accepts the initialization-only step value.** It reported
  result 7 after 36 ms on both boards, and `init_DRAM` reached the size line
  after 40 ms; the simple test then failed, because DRAM was untrained.
- **The `0xa0000` block is left out of the set.** Between two
  P-state-0-only lifetimes of one board, 3,474 of the 3,575 words of its
  P-state 0 copy changed, mostly by one or two bits, including words that
  boot0 writes with fixed values. That behaviour is neither configuration
  nor a training result; its function needs the vendor reference, and the
  restore relies on boot0 rewriting the block on its own path.
- **The restore sets agree.** Without that block, the P-state-0-only minus
  initialization-only diff holds 1,026 registers on 3-3 and 1,052 on 3-1,
  1,008 of them on both. The set is derived by one recorded command over
  all twenty captures, per board and united, with status pooled over both
  boards and with firmware controls, firmware inputs and controller
  read-result words left out.
- **Byte-lane status is decided per register offset.** The byte lanes share
  one register map, so an offset that is status in any lane is left out in
  every lane: `0xe0`, `0xe2`, `0xe8` and `0x1c4`, status in the lanes of
  byte blocks 0 and 1. Offset `0xe6` (register `0x73`) is left out in every
  lane because it does not hold a written value: on port 3-1 the restore
  wrote 6 to lane 0 and read 0 in all bits, after nineteen registers of the
  same lane had read back their written values. Its trained value is the
  same in every trained capture of both boards, a property of hardware
  status ([runbook](../board-runbooks/dram-restore-test-1.md#the-first-board-run-stopped-at-a-byte-lane-register-that-does-not-hold-a-write)).
- **Registers the PHY owns are left out** because a write survey on port
  3-1 showed that they do not keep an APB write at the hook
  ([runbook](../board-runbooks/dram-restore-test-1.md#the-survey-run-separated-wide-memory-words-from-registers-the-phy-owns)):
  - byte-lane offset `0x11e` in every lane, a copy that the PHY updates from
    offset `0x4c` (lane 0) or `0x4e` (lane 1 from lane 0);
  - byte-lane offsets `0x1aa`–`0x1be` and `0x130`, values the PHY produces,
    which differ between lifetimes of the same kind, also after
    initialization only;
  - offsets `0x15e`–`0x17c` of the two blocks at CSR `0x30000` and
    `0x31000` (`0x0a960000`, `0x0a962000`), and `0x0a940014`, values of the
    same kind.
- **The set has 899 registers:** 402 byte-lane registers, 445
  address/command sequencer (ACSM) words, 10 registers of the two
  `0x30000`-region blocks, 20 message-block fields, 20 parameter words and
  two others. The
  [first test's runbook](../board-runbooks/dram-restore-test-1.md) lists the
  exclusions and their reasons.
- **The chip IDs differ in their last word only** (`0x40892413` on 3-3,
  `0x40792413` on 3-1). Trained byte-lane values differ between the boards
  by a median of 2 codes, so a record belongs to one board, as the chip-ID
  check requires.

The last reconnect of 2026-10-25 added a four-P-state lifetime per board, which confirms the status class (`0x0a51022c`, already status on 3-1) and shows that the `0xa0000` block is mostly stable after four-P-state training but not after P-state-0-only training. No further lifetime is available, so the set is fixed from these lifetimes; [the first test's runbook](../board-runbooks/dram-restore-test-1.md) gives the set's derivation, the build it needs, the predictions, the qualification ladder and the residual risk. Until cold and warm lifetimes exist, a record is valid only for room-temperature cold starts.
narrative:
**The first lifetime.** Two four-P-state captures of one port 3-3 lifetime (`board-session-20261025-21`) agree on 84,095 registers and differ on 274 status registers: 207 in the APB-only block, 64 byte-lane registers at offsets `0xe0`, `0xe2`, `0xe8` and `0x1c4` of the eight lanes of byte blocks
0 and 1 only, two master registers (`0x0a940176`, `0x0a940178`) and one DRTUB register (`0x0aa80206`). The status lane registers appear only in blocks 0 and 1, which suggests that one channel's tracking runs between the captures. All 49,152 registers of `0x0000`–`0xbfff` read zero, so the address/command delays are not where the published PHY keeps them; the restore set must come from the blocks boot0 accesses or from the kind 2 and kind 3 diff. `UcclkHclkEnables` read 0 after training. `analyse-ddr-captures.py` output: `~/.cache/sunstoneos/evidence/dram-training-analysis-20261025/port-3-3-lifetime-1-blocks.json`.

**The first P-state-0-only lifetime** (`board-session-20261025-25`) and the four-P-state lifetime differ in 13,717 registers (`dram-training-analysis-20261025/port-3-3-two-lifetimes.json`). They fall into two groups:

- **Programmed differently for the two kinds, about 13,500:** every one of
  the four `0xa0000` copies (about 3,300 each), 163 address/command
  sequencer words that move between positions, twelve master registers
  shifted by exactly `0x38`, the multi-P-state message-block fields at
  `0x0a9b00f0`–`0x0a9b041a` (zero after the P-state-0-only run), byte 4 of
  the message block (`0xa0` against `0x30`, as predicted) and seven
  controller words. boot0 writes these itself on the restore's own path, so
  they are configuration and stay out of the restore set; the `0xa0000`
  block behaves like sequence memory loaded per kind.
- **Training results, about 250:** 219 byte-lane registers, 186 of which
  moved by at most 4 codes (lane offsets `0x20`–`0x26`, `0x40`–`0x42`,
  `0x4c`–`0x4e`, `0x9c`–`0x9e` and `0x1a4`–`0x1be`), the message-block result
  fields at `0x0a9b0036`–`0x0a9b0058` and `0x0a9b00d0`–`0x0a9b00de`, three
  master registers (`0x0a940058`–`0x0a940060`, `0x82f` against `0x833`), six
  `0x30000` registers, controller word `0x0a020040` (`0x2f2f` against
  `0x2e2e`, the MR14 pattern) and parameter words 32–51.
 The training-step value at `0x0a9b0010` read `0x125f` in both kinds.

conclusion: The SID-selected default passed twice on port 3-1 on 2026-10-31 with quick checks of 34.116 and 34.117 ms (estimated 30 ms), 879 PHY writes, 12,288 MiB reported and clock_point_result 0. Explicit-record restores passed on both boards. hypothesis: A WDT0 system reset returns a board to a new FEL instance without a replug, so a failed restore can fall back to one full training.
narrative: WDT0 register order measured on both boards on 2026-10-31: output 2, configuration 1 (system reset), mode 0x41 (enabled, four seconds) and restart word 0x14af, all under key 0x16aa0000, with readback. The board left USB about 4.2 s after arming and a new FEL instance enumerated at about 5.9 s (a reset costs about 6 s). The mode register keeps 0x41 through the reset. The plain wrapper's code equals the code that trained both boards to 12,288 MiB on the instances the reset created. The runner writes no RTC FEL flag or ROM redirect word, as in the measurement. Evidence: ~/.cache/sunstoneos/evidence/wdt-fel-return-20261031/ and ~/.cache/sunstoneos/evidence/resume-20261031b/.

hypothesis: The derived card boot0 and its 10,120-byte helper select, fall back and fail terminally as designed under modeled boot0 and MMIO.
conclusion: Host and instruction checks pass; they model MMIO and stop at the terminal WFE, and establish neither physical timing, ROM acceptance nor DRAM margins. No card boot has run.
narrative:
The current offline evidence is in `~/.cache/sunstoneos/evidence/dram-restore-1031b/` (`card-restore`, `card-default` and their check directories). The experimental boot0 SHA-256 is `0a25e1ceaa79242702eff2b9758070f1db8022348d29d8c2cd7094e1a7d5ea11`; the default image is `78d5056f3313ceadd3323010daf67fc1f4e88dba190888d1a76c57ac2ccf5182`. Both load the same 10,120-byte helper, SHA-256 `9ff8be424035314edd0e9da9a784cd1916ae4483a1c57347cbd636433d7ac08e`, which includes the shared quick check. Its single initialized section occupies `0x92000..0x94a3c`. Bootstrap sections use 120, 76, 72, 64, 124, 80, 20 and 112 bytes in slots 8–15. Every section fits after its zero presence word; no raw-loader BSS is admitted.
 `checks/card-ddr.py` passed twenty experimental cases and the default fallback case. It executes selection, fallback and terminal failures with modeled boot0 training and MMIO. It checks original arguments, stack and callee-saved registers, four fallback timing calls, helper/record corruption, wrong-board rejection and stop-before-continuation after partial restore. `checks/card-ddr-pio.py` executes the pinned PIO wait instructions and the actual timer shim: thirteen cases include inactive-timer equivalence, low-word wrap, slow FIFO progress, command/data/reset/clock-reset expiry and a direct busy-loop check. `checks/card-ddr-host.py` passed nineteen cases covering the actual producer, package/parser, exact helper ranges, stale/torn resume refusal and preserved backup. The default instruction case performs no restore reads. These checks model MMIO and stop at the terminal `WFE`; they do not establish physical timing, ROM acceptance or DRAM margins.
 For the actual record, the first valid helper uses 20 sectors and the two records use 50 sectors: 35,840 bytes read. A bad first helper followed by a valid second uses 46,080 bytes. The format caps both-helper/both-record reads at 226 sectors, or 115,712 bytes. One non-refreshable ten-second counter budget covers the attempt. Restore performs 879 masked PHY writes and up to
89 rewrites of other wide-memory halfwords, a readback pass, and a separate
879-read final pass. The quick check writes and reads 262,392 bytes each way. The instruction fixture caps each case at five million instructions; the largest observed case uses 4,541,947. This count is not a hardware performance measure.

A missing, corrupt, stale, wrong-board or otherwise ineligible record calls the original `init_DRAM` once with the original parameters. The inactive timing trampoline preserves boot0's normal training path. After restore starts, a readback, size or sampled-memory failure stores its error in SRAM and stops without returning to boot0 or retraining. No warm-reset or autonomous recovery destination is assumed.
 Current records have unknown capture temperature and no qualified thermal range. The default derived image therefore falls back to full training. An explicitly requested experimental build may exercise the existing room-temperature restore profile, with false physical/thermal qualification fields in its manifest. It has no runtime temperature measurement. That build is an offline prototype, not permission to boot a board; physical use still requires the supervised cold-start and memory-test prerequisites. Runtime temperature admission needs new capture data before a production card-restore policy can be enabled.

hypothesis: The qualification ladder, periodic retraining and the wider Part A and Part B checks establish a restore safe for card deployment.
prediction:
## Periodic retraining every N boots
 A boot counter must survive power removal without a card write on every boot. The OS keeps the count in its data partition, which section 4 permits once the card has a host backup and the image confines its writes there. When the count reaches N, the OS clears the record header through the backup-first path, and the next boot trains fully; a capture of the restore set after that training produces the new record. Until a native backup-first writer is qualified, the coordinator does both steps from the host. N comes from the drift data: the number of boots, or the time and temperature span, over which restored values stay within the spread of fresh trainings.
 ## Qualification before any card write

0. **P-state 0 only**, both boards: full training of P-state 0 alone, its
   timing, the March C- run of the
   [memory qualification image](../memory-qualification.md), and the
   reference captures.
1. **Captures** of all three kinds on both boards, several lifetimes each
   and two temperatures, analysed; the restore set, masks and mode-register
   list frozen and reviewed.
2. **FEL restore prototype**, port 3-3 then 3-1: the device-initialization
   run, then restored boots, each followed by the full March C- run and a
   stress run, hot (after sustained CPU and memory load) and cold (after a
   long power-off at room temperature or below). Any bit error stops the
   work.
3. **Fallback cases** on the FEL path: a wrong CRC, another board's chip ID,
   a changed strap CRC, a temperature limit of zero, a forced read-back
   mismatch and a forced quick-check failure. Pre-admission rejection must leave parameters
   unchanged and run full training once. Post-edit readback and memory failures
   must stop before caller continuation, with no in-place retraining; on the
   FEL path the runner then resets through WDT0 and trains fully once.
4. **Boot time**: ten restored and ten fully trained boots per board,
   comparing boot0's `DRAM BOOT DRIVE INFO` to `Actual DRAM SIZE` interval.
5. **Card**: host backup, record write through the new region, then the
   card-boot variant repeats steps 2–4.

Budget predictions: DRAM interval with restore 500 ms (prediction about 70 ms); card pre-admission fallback one full training in the same boot, about 5.1 s plus successful reads; FEL fallback one WDT0 reset (about 6 s) and one four-P-state training (about 5.1 s).
conclusion: Not yet run beyond the FEL restores in dram-training-restore-default-1031. The ladder steps for full-map March C- after restore, repeated and temperature lifetimes, fallback cases on the board and card deployment remain open; the design doc lists them as open work.
narrative:
**Future qualification proposal, not implemented.** The wider Part A/Part B checks and RTC reset policy below need separate design and physical evidence. The accepted implementation uses the uncached 8 KiB check described under RAM-only restore and terminal failure behavior; it does not implement this reset proposal.
 Part A, in the AArch32 hook below 4 GiB: a short burst test per channel, rank and byte lane with walking-ones and pseudo-random patterns over 1 MiB per rank, written with cached `LDM`/`STM` bursts after the cache setup that boot0's parser uses, then cleaned and invalidated by address (`DCCIMVAC`) before the read phase, so that the reads reach DRAM and not the cluster caches. Part B, in the stage-2 monitor at EL3: the same pattern and cache maintenance (`DC CIVAC`) over the 12,288 MiB map, one
64 KiB window per 256 MiB, excluding the monitor's own image. After a restored boot, part B failing sets a retrain flag in an RTC general-purpose register other than indexes 1 and 2, which boot0 uses (`0x4a940`, `0x4a95c`), and requests a warm reset. After a full-training boot, part B failing stops with a report and no reset, so a bad full training cannot loop. The flag is cleared only when part B passes. The check catches gross restore errors only. Marginal timing shows only in the qualification runs, and the safety of the restore rests on them.
